$comment: Framework-owned size budgets. Raising a number here is a reviewed diff, which is the point: a budget CI can quietly exceed is a wish, not a budget. Bytes are uncompressed, because that is what a build can measure without guessing a host's compression settings. See src/artifact/budgets.ts for what separates the three groups and why the emitted HTML - not the module graph - is what decides.

basePage.note:
What every visitor downloads before interacting, on the heaviest single page. MEASURED against tests/helpers/consumer.ts - a portal with a Data Browser, an auth island, a documentation tree with code and mathematics, a themed preset and a catalogue of thirty datasets: JavaScript 571,801 and CSS 95,690, where the JavaScript figure now includes the chunks the page's own script STATICALLY imports and not only the ones its HTML names - a distinction that had been hiding 380 KB.

THE CSS CEILING WAS RAISED, from 122,880 to 131,072, AND THE BASE PAGE WAS REDUCED. Both, because either alone would have been the wrong answer. A consumer-shaped portal measured 123,890 bytes of base CSS with no Python enabled at all - 1,010 over the old ceiling - after two unconditional stylesheets grew by 22,229 bytes between releases (the shell's own by 14,873, the dataset-tree block wrapper's by 7,356). A base-page budget the base page cannot meet is not a budget, and splitting the optional playground out into its own budget, which is the rest of this file, would not have moved that number by a single byte.

The reduction: @freva-org/dataset-tree's own stylesheet is no longer a `<link>` in every page's head. It styles only markup the island draws, so it is imported `?inline` and adopted through a constructable stylesheet at mount time, and the island itself is now reached through a literal dynamic import gated on a block being on the page. Measured on the fixture, that is 17,638 fewer bytes of eager CSS and 41,305 fewer of eager JavaScript, on every page - including the 404 document and every documentation page, which had been paying for a tree they do not have. It brings the consumer measurement back under even the retired ceiling.

So why raise it at all? Because 122,880 was never a measured number and the last two releases both crossed it. 131,072 is 8 KiB of deliberate headroom above a ceiling the reduction has already cleared, not a number chosen to make a failing build pass. What remains eager and is the next honest target is the shell stylesheet itself, 91,271 bytes minified, which includes the mathematics rules that every page links whether or not it has a formula on it. That one is not a bundler flag either: Astro hoists the CSS of anything reachable from a page's client graph, deliberately, so making it lazy means moving it off that graph.

python-playground.note:
RAISED FROM 655,360 TO 688,128 (672 KiB), for structured startup failures.

WHAT CROSSED IT. A portal whose ONLY optional feature is the playground - no Data Browser, no dataset tree - measured 660,996 bytes, 5,636 over. That shape is the worst case for this ceiling and it is the shape `browser-tests/python-deployment.mjs` builds: attribution is first-wins over the chunk graph, so with nothing else enabled the playground claims every shared chunk itself, including the console's jQuery Terminal and Prism. The same commit measures well under the ceiling on the consumer fixture and on a Waterpark-shaped portal, both of which have a Data Browser to claim those chunks first. This is the shape-dependence docs/design/lazy-budget-shape.md describes; the ceiling is raised for the worst shape rather than tuned for the convenient one.

WHAT THE BYTES BOUGHT. `src/worker/startup-failure.ts` and the rendering it does: a start failure now carries which resource class failed, the add-on it was about, the URL, the HTTP status, the configuration key that selects that location - by its portal name AND its API name - the command that produces the files, and whether retrying can help. The message it produces replaces one that named a URL and a status and left a reader to guess the rest, and that ended with an `Underlying error:` that was usually empty because Pyodide's messages end in a newline. The same module renders the optional-add-on report the ready payload carries.

672 KiB is 27,132 bytes of headroom above the measurement - roughly what this round added, again - chosen the same way the Data Browser's ceiling was: enough that a round of ordinary diagnostic work does not have to come back here, small enough that a feature arriving whole still has to be looked at.

lazy.note:
Emitted code no page asks for, fetched only when something needs it. Bounded because 'it is lazy' is a reason to weigh it differently and not a reason to stop weighing it: a lazy chunk is still a download, still a parse, and still bytes a deployment serves.

MEASURED on the consumer fixture with the playground enabled: 770,262 bytes in total, of which the Python playground is 533,459 - the console with jQuery Terminal and Prism (380,142), the interpreter's Worker (132,692), the coordinator (11,886) and the two-origin bridge (8,739) - the dataset-tree island 59,430, and the Data Browser's metadata tables 177,073. The playground's own ceiling is stated separately so that growth in one optional feature cannot be paid for out of another's headroom.

Attribution follows the bundler's own edges, not only module ownership. The console's private libraries - jQuery, jQuery Terminal, Prism - are third-party modules no evidence plan owns, and before the edges were followed they were 269 KB charged to nobody at all, which is the exact shape of the exemption this model exists to refuse.

THE CEILING WAS RAISED FROM 917,504 TO 983,040, for one deliberate feature, and the accounting was tightened in the same change rather than loosened.

WHAT CROSSED IT. A Waterpark deployment with the Data Browser enabled alongside a LIVE dataset tree measures 936,720 bytes of lazily loaded JavaScript, 19,216 over the old ceiling. The cause is not drift: the round that restored the tree's own behaviour gave every real Zarr store an Inspect action, and that opens '@freva-org/data-inspector' IN THE PAGE rather than sending a reader to a raw storage URL. Its chunk measures 43,420 bytes, with a further 572 for the loader module that is the only thing naming it - so the feature is more than twice the overage on its own, and a portal that had it would have crossed 917,504 whatever else it enabled.

WHAT IT COSTS A READER: NOTHING, until they press Inspect. The inspector is referenced by no page, so it is in no page's <link> or <script> tags and adds zero bytes to the base page - measured, on the consumer fixture with the Data Browser, a live tree and the playground: base-page JavaScript 576,099 against a ceiling of 786,432, unchanged by the inspector's presence. That is the whole argument for raising a LAZY ceiling and it would not support raising the base-page one.

MEASURED HERE, on the same fixture: 841,284 bytes of lazy JavaScript in total, of which the playground is 419,172 in chunks plus a 132,692 Worker, the Data Browser 177,073 and the dataset tree 110,896 - the island (55,480), the inspector (43,420), the S3 adapter (10,014), the access recipes (1,410) and the inspector's loader (572). The fixture is smaller than the deployment that crossed the ceiling because it enables neither the STAC Browser nor as many routes; 983,040 is 46,320 above the deployment's own figure, which is roughly one more feature of the inspector's size, and not a number chosen to make one build pass.

AND THE TIGHTENING. The inspector and its loader used to be attributed to nothing at all: they were lazy bytes with no feature against their name, so the tree's cost read as its island alone and 43,992 bytes only became visible as an aggregate ceiling failing in somebody's build. They are now owned by the dataset-tree evidence plan, which charges them to that feature and makes 'a portal with no dataset tree contains no inspector' a checked claim under FP1601. The per-feature ceilings are unchanged, the base-page ceilings are unchanged, and nothing was exempted.

RAISED AGAIN, TO 1,048,576, AND PER-FEATURE CEILINGS WERE TRIED AND WITHDRAWN IN THE SAME CHANGE. A consumer build measured 983,497 bytes, 457 over. Two raises in three rounds is the shape of a budget that is not doing its job, and `docs/design/lazy-budget-shape.md` already says why - so the first attempt at this was the fix that document proposes: hard ceilings for `dataset-tree` and `data` beside the playground's, with this total derived as their sum plus an unattributed allowance. It does not work yet, and the reason is worth recording where the next person will find it.

ATTRIBUTION IS NOT STABLE ACROSS DEPLOYMENT SHAPES. The edge walk claims a shared chunk for the first feature that can reach it, so what a feature WEIGHS depends on what else is enabled beside it. Measured, on the same commit: the dataset tree is 139,424 bytes in a portal that also has the Data Browser and the playground, and 321,219 in one that has the tree and the playground alone - the same code, 2.3 times the number, because with no Data Browser to claim them first the terminal's chunks fall to the tree. A per-feature ceiling that is right for one portal is wrong for the next one, and shipping it would fail builds in shapes nobody measured. That is a second, sharper argument for the redesign and a reason not to do half of it by hand.

So the aggregate is raised and nothing else changed. 1,048,576 is 65,079 above the build that crossed it - about one more chunk the size of the inspector - which is the same kind of headroom the last raise used and the same kind of number: measured, then rounded up by roughly one feature.

MEASURED on the consumer fixture with a live tree, the Data Browser and the playground: 877,331 in total - python-playground 560,834, the Data Browser 177,073 and the dataset tree 139,424, with nothing left over. Add the `cosmos` preset, which is the shape the build that crossed the ceiling had, and the same fixture measures 983,497: the same figure the consumer reported, to the byte. The scene's engine is 106,166 of it, and the walk charges it to the Data Browser - it belongs to a theme, and a theme owns no evidence plan. The playground's own ceiling is unchanged and still has 94 KB of headroom.

WHAT GREW, AND WHY IT IS NOT DRIFT. The dataset tree went from 110,896 to 139,424, and 20,278 of that is `@freva-org/data-inspector`: its chunk was 43,420 when the portal imported the package for its custom element alone and never called it, and it is 63,698 now that Inspect actually reads the store - `openDatasetMeta`, `buildXarrayRepr` and the repr's stylesheet were tree-shaken out of a feature that did not work. The rest is this round's own additions to the island, the inspector's host module and the terminal's chrome. A reader pays none of it until they press Inspect, and the base page is unchanged: 577,372 against a ceiling of 786,432 on the same fixture.

AND THE FAILURE NOW SAYS WHERE THE BYTES ARE. `FP1407` on this total prints the per-feature breakdown, because '983497 is above 983040' is a true sentence that answers nothing in somebody else's CI - the report had the numbers and was keeping them to itself.

databrowser.note:
MEASURED, and raised once. A consumer-shaped portal with a Data Browser, a live dataset tree and the Python playground measured 784,897 bytes here before this round's terminal work and 786,817 after it - 385 over the retired ceiling of 786,432, on a margin that had been 1,535. The round added about 1.9 KB: hover text on the three session rows, a submenu that measures itself against the viewport before it opens, and the two handlers that let a reader drag a line out of the transcript instead of having the gesture cancelled under them.

READ THE NAME WITH CARE. A component is charged for the modules it OWNS, and ownership is first-wins over the chunk graph (see `featureOf` in src/artifact/budgets.ts): the Data Browser is the first component in a Waterpark-shaped portal's evidence, so it claims every shared chunk that nothing has claimed yet - the dataset tree, the terminal window, the console. None of the 1.9 KB is Data Browser code. That is the same shape-dependence that made the per-feature lazy ceilings unkeepable and got them withdrawn last round; see docs/design/lazy-budget-shape.md.

776 KiB is 7,807 bytes of headroom above the measurement, chosen the same way the base-page CSS ceiling was: enough that a round of ordinary interface work does not have to come back here, small enough that a feature arriving whole still has to be looked at.

externalRuntime.note: Pyodide, its standard library and any wheels a profile installs. NOT ENFORCED, and not because it is small: it is by far the largest thing a playground costs. It is not enforced because this build does not emit it and cannot measure it - the interpreter is fetched at run time from the CDN that @freva-org/browser-python pins, and a number a build cannot measure is not a gate, it is a comment with a colon in it. It is recorded here so a reviewer weighing the feature sees the whole cost rather than the part that happens to be countable.
externalRuntime.pyodideRuntimeAndStdlib: 12.8 MB, 6.0 MB gzipped, on the first start()
externalRuntime.profileXarrayZarr: a further 9.6 MB across 17 wheels, on the first start()
externalRuntime.profileFrevaClient: a further 178 KiB for the derived Freva wheel, plus whatever micropip resolves from PyPI, on the first start()
externalRuntime.when: Never during page load. Only when an interpreter is actually started - which is what `dataset-tree.python.autostart` decides.
